lesson.title: Demonstratives & Stressed Pronouns
lesson.subtitle: Pointing with ce/cet/cette/ces and standing alone after prepositions with moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous.

hook.title: Pointers (ce/cet/cette/ces) and Stressed Pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle)
hook.content: One French pointer family covers both 'this' and 'that': ce (masculine consonant: ce livre), cet (masculine vowel/mute H: cet hôtel, cet ami), cette (feminine: cette ville), and ces (plural: ces livres)! And after any preposition (avec, pour, sans, chez) or C'est, pronouns wear their stressed coats: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous!

footnotes.title: How cet and cette sound 100% identical (/sɛt/)
footnotes.content: Masculine prevocalic cet (/sɛt/) and feminine cette (/sɛt/) sound completely identical in speech!

pattern.title: ce / cet / cette / ces before Nouns; moi / toi / lui / elle after Prepositions
pattern.content: Use cet before masculine vowels/mute H, and use moi/toi/lui/elle after avec, pour, chez.
pattern.linguist_note: French stressed (disjunctive) pronouns moi, toi, lui descend from Latin tonic oblique forms mē, tē, illūi.
pattern.trap_note: Never write *ce hôtel or *avec je — use cet hôtel and avec moi!

exercises.prompt: Match each pointer or stressed pronoun phrase with its meaning:

matching_pairs.german: at his place / at her place

exercises.target_answer: this / that book, this / that hotel, friend, this / that city, with me / for you, at his place / at her place
exercises.meaning: ce livre (masculine consonant), cet hôtel / cet ami (masculine vowel/H), cette ville (feminine), avec moi / pour toi, chez lui / chez elle
exercises.explanation: cet prevents a vowel collision in the masculine; moi/toi/lui/elle follow prepositions.

exercises.prompt: Which demonstrative correctly completes '___ homme et ___ femme' ('this man and this woman')?
exercises.meaning: this man (cet before mute H) and this woman (cette, f.)
exercises.explanation: homme is masculine and starts with a mute H, so ce becomes cet: cet homme.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'This coffee is for me, and that cake is for you (informal)'?
options: Ce café est pour moi et ce gâteau est pour toi
Cette café est pour moi et cette gâteau est pour toi
Ce café est pour me et ce gâteau est pour te
exercises.target_answer: Ce café est pour moi et ce gâteau est pour toi
exercises.meaning: This coffee is for me and that cake is for you
exercises.explanation: After a preposition like pour, me/te become stressed moi/toi!

exercises.idea: I am coming with you to this hotel
cues: I am coming with you → Je viens avec toi
to this hotel → à cet hôtel
idea_parts: verb + companion → Je viens avec toi
exercises.target_answer: Je viens avec toi à cet hôtel
exercises.meaning: I am coming with you to this hotel
exercises.explanation: avec takes stressed toi, and masculine mute-H hôtel takes cet.

diagnosis.cue: Use avec toi and à cet hôtel.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: C'est pour moi ou c'est pour lui
exercises.target_answer: C'est pour moi ou c'est pour lui
exercises.meaning: Is it for me or is it for him?
cues: or for him: ou c'est pour lui
exercises.explanation: After pour, use stressed moi and lui.
exercises.affirmation: You used both stressed pronouns moi and lui after pour.

summary.outcome: Point at nouns with ce, cet, cette, ces and use stressed pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous) after prepositions.

use_example.german: Cet hôtel est très beau — tu viens avec moi ?
use_example.english: This hotel is very beautiful — are you coming with me?

summary.takeaway: ce becomes cet before a masculine vowel, and prepositions always take moi, toi, lui, elle.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([15] Numbers & the Four-Twenties): see how Demonstratives & Stressed Pronouns leads directly into Numbers & the Four-Twenties.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I am coming with you to this hotel" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je viens avec toi à cet hôtel
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je viens avec toi à cet hôtel" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Demonstratives & Stressed Pronouns.

ce.etymology_derivation: Becomes cet before a vowel (cet hôtel) and cette in the feminine (cette table).

moi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions (avec moi, chez moi, pour moi) and in C'est moi.

toi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions: pour toi, chez toi.

lui.context_translation: I speak to him / to her.
lui.etymology_derivation: One single pronoun means BOTH 'to him' and 'to her' before a verb!

nous.etymology_derivation: Latin nōs — English keeps the root in nostrum.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

avec.etymology_derivation: ab hoc 'by this' wore into avec. No English twin — but 'with' itself once meant 'against', so prepositions travel too.

pour.etymology_derivation: Followed by an infinitive, pour means 'in order to': pour comprendre ('in order to understand').

chez.etymology_derivation: Latin casa 'hut, house' — the same house English visits in casino (literally 'little house'). No English twin: an honest loss.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

livre.etymology_derivation: Masculine le livre is 'the book'; feminine la livre is 'the pound'!
